article_title: Community Schools in Rural California: Leveraging Shared Resources in West Kern County
citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: MQI virtual math coaching
description: The consortium adopted Harvard University's Mathematical Quality of Instruction (MQI) coaching, described as "a program that engages math educators in virtual and video-based coaching cycles." A participating teacher films a math lesson, the coach reviews it and provides individualized feedback, and may refer the teacher to the MQI video library. The consortium used it to maximize access to and frequency of math coaching that was previously unavailable and unaffordable to the individual small districts.
requirements: Grant resources to fund access to the external coaching program, which individual districts could not previously afford.
target_learners: K–8 math teachers in small rural districts
examples: Consortium leaders invested in math coaches as a primary means of spurring academic improvement; none of the districts had access to math coaches before receiving community school grants.
key_sources: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620

article_title: Using Tablets to Explore the Potential for Video-Based Classroom Observations for Research and Professional Development
citation: Blazar, D., Gilbert, B., Herlihy, C., & Gogolen, C. (2018). Using tablets to explore the potential for video-based classroom observations for research and professional development. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology (IJEMST), 6(2), 122-135. https://doi.org/10.18404/ijemst.408935
title: MQI Coaching Cycle: describe, elevate, then select next steps over short video clips
description: A recurring two-week coaching routine in which teacher and coach analyze three short clips — two of the teacher's own instruction and one exemplar from the MQI video library. The conversation follows a fixed structure: "describe, then elevate, then select next steps", keeping talk focused on one or two MQI codes at a time so teachers leave with concrete instructional next steps. The article presents this as the mechanism by which video and the rubric produce focused, high-quality coaching conversations.
requirements: Coaches require advanced mathematical content knowledge and substantial initial plus ongoing training and oversight to facilitate the conversations
constraints: Facilitating high-quality conversations is described as not an easy task and dependent on training, planning, and preparation
target_learners: elementary and middle grades mathematics teachers (grades 3-8)
target_learning_goals: improve mathematics instruction on MQI domains such as richness of the mathematics and Common Core-aligned student practices
examples: In the pilot, coaches were certified MQI raters; each session discussed one stock video and two clips of the teacher's own classroom
key_sources: Blazar, D., Gilbert, B., Herlihy, C., & Gogolen, C. (2018). Using tablets to explore the potential for video-based classroom observations for research and professional development. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology (IJEMST), 6(2), 122-135. https://doi.org/10.18404/ijemst.408935

article_title: Virtual Reality Versus In-Person Simulation of Sepsis for Medical Students: Randomized Comparative Pilot Study.
citation: Medwell Lauren, Old Tim, Ahmed Awais, Holloway Victoria, McTaggart Lauren, Morgan Dafydd, O'Keeffe Callum, Olori Jemaima, Payne Ellie, Rainforth Christopher, Ramanujam Namritha, Vaidya Kriti, Jacobs Chris (2026). Virtual Reality Versus In-Person Simulation of Sepsis for Medical Students: Randomized Comparative Pilot Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/80316
title: Modified Queen's Simulation Assessment Tool (mQSAT) for cross-modality simulation performance assessment
description: The mQSAT quantified simulation performance in this study using 5 Likert-style scales ranging from inferior (1) to superior (5) performance, four rating primary assessment, diagnostic actions, therapeutic actions and communication, plus a global rating. Two unblinded authors marked all simulations; assessment simulations were additionally video-recorded and double-marked by two blinded assessors randomly allocated from the other study authors.
requirements: guide statements presented together with each Likert-style scale
the tool is validated for use in the assessment of IP simulation performance of medical students with good interrater reliability
constraints: The mQSAT tool, though validated for IP simulation assessment, has not been previously validated for VR simulation scenarios
target_learning_goals: assessment of simulation performance across primary assessment, diagnostic actions, therapeutic actions, and communication domains
examples: In this pilot, two unblinded authors marked all teaching and assessment simulations, and two blinded assessors additionally double-marked the video-recorded assessment simulations
